text: Confirm the shape of it: `top` (press `1` to show per-core usage). One core is pegged at 100% while others sit idle, yet `render-worker` is still crawling -- that combination (a busy process, but low overall box usage) usually points at CPU *affinity*, not a CPU quota or priority problem.

Check what core render-worker is actually allowed to run on: find its PID (`cat /var/run/render-worker/render-worker.pid`), then `taskset -p <pid>`. Compare that against what's hogging the busy core: `taskset -p <pid-of-whatever-top-shows-on-that-core>`.

Both land on the same CPU mask. `render-worker` is pinned there by its own config (`/etc/render-worker/render-worker.conf`, `PINNED_CORE=`), a leftover from old tuning -- and a separate, legitimate workload (`batch-encoder`) has permanently and correctly claimed that exact core for itself. render-worker doesn't need that specific core; it just needs *a* free one.

Stop forcing it onto a contended core: edit `/etc/render-worker/render-worker.conf`, clear `PINNED_CORE=` (leave the value empty), then `sudo svc-ctl restart`. With no pin, the scheduler puts it on whatever core is actually free. You can confirm live without restarting anything, too: `sudo taskset -pc 1 <pid>` (or any core other than whatever `batch-encoder` is on) re-pins a running process's affinity immediately.
